name: Yield, Atom Economy and Green Chemistry
what: Percentage yield measures how much of the theoretical maximum product was actually obtained from a reaction. Percentage atom economy measures what proportion of the reactant atoms end up in the desired product. Green chemistry principles guide the design of safer, more efficient and more sustainable chemical processes.
why: These concepts are essential for evaluating whether a chemical process is efficient, cost-effective and environmentally responsible. They are heavily assessed in VCE Chemistry Unit 4 and link directly to real-world industrial and environmental contexts.

items.title: I can calculate the percentage yield of a single-step reaction given the actual yield and the mass of a reactant
items.what: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100. The theoretical yield is calculated from the stoichiometry of the balanced equation using the moles of the limiting reagent. The actual yield is the mass of product actually obtained after the reaction.
items.why: Percentage yield tells chemists how efficiently a reaction converts starting materials into the desired product. A low yield indicates significant waste or side reactions.
items.example: 45 g of ethanol (0.98 mol) is oxidised to ethanoic acid. Theoretical yield = 0.98 mol × 60 g/mol = 58.7 g. If 38 g is obtained, percentage yield = (38/58.7) × 100 = 65%.

items.title: I can calculate the mass of product formed when the percentage yield and mass of starting material are known
items.what: First calculate the theoretical yield using stoichiometry, then multiply by the fractional percentage yield: actual yield = (percentage yield / 100) × theoretical yield.
items.why: This calculation is used in industrial settings to predict how much product a process will deliver, which informs decisions about scale-up and cost.
items.example: But-2-ene + Br2 at 93% yield. 35 g of but-2-ene (0.625 mol) gives a theoretical yield of 135 g of product. Actual yield = 0.93 × 135 = 125 g.

items.title: I can calculate the overall percentage yield of a multi-step reaction pathway
items.what: The overall percentage yield of a multi-step pathway is found by multiplying the individual percentage yields of each step together. For example, for three steps with yields of 29%, 89% and 72%: overall yield = 0.29 × 0.89 × 0.72 × 100 = 19%.
items.why: Multi-step pathways accumulate yield losses at every step. Understanding this discourages unnecessarily long synthesis routes and motivates chemists to develop more efficient pathways.
items.example: A three-step synthesis of propanoic acid with step yields of 29%, 89% and 72% gives an overall yield of 0.29 × 0.89 × 0.72 × 100 = 19%.

items.title: I can calculate the percentage atom economy of a single-step reaction
items.what: Percentage atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / total molar mass of all products) × 100. Since mass is conserved, the denominator can also be written as the total molar mass of all reactants. Catalysts and solvents are not included.
items.why: Atom economy measures how wasteful a reaction is at the molecular level. A reaction with 100% atom economy (like a pure addition reaction) produces no by-products at all.
items.example: For CH3CH2CH2Cl + NH3 → CH3CH2CH2NH2 + HCl: M(desired product) = 59 g/mol, M(all products) = 59 + 36.5 = 95.5 g/mol. Atom economy = (59/95.5) × 100 = 61.8%.

items.title: I can calculate the percentage atom economy of a multi-step reaction pathway
items.what: For a multi-step pathway, the atom economy is calculated using all reactants added across every step (the starting organic material plus every reagent added in subsequent steps) in the denominator, and the molar mass of the final desired product in the numerator. The main organic compound is not double-counted.
items.why: Calculating pathway atom economy reveals the cumulative waste potential of a synthesis. Long pathways using stoichiometric reagents tend to have very low atom economy.
items.example: Pathway: ethane + Br2 (UV) → bromoethane + NH3 → ethanamine. Reactants: M(C2H6) + M(Br2) + M(NH3) = 30 + 159.8 + 17 = 206.8 g/mol. Atom economy = (45/206.8) × 100 = 21.8%.

items.title: I can discuss the advantages for society and industry of developing chemical processes with a high percentage atom economy
items.what: High atom economy means fewer by-products are formed. This reduces waste disposal costs and environmental impact, improves product purity (fewer by-products to separate), reduces hazard exposure for workers, and lowers the overall cost of production.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to go beyond simply stating that fewer by-products are produced and to explain the downstream consequences for environment, safety, cost and product quality.
items.example: A reaction with 95% atom economy produces far less waste than one with 40% atom economy. This means the 95% process requires less waste treatment infrastructure, is cheaper to run and poses lower risks to workers handling the materials.

items.title: I can explain how the use of renewable feedstocks contributes to sustainable chemical production
items.what: Renewable feedstocks are raw materials that can be replenished faster than they are consumed, such as plant biomass, animal fats or waste materials. Using them reduces dependence on finite fossil fuel resources and can reduce waste by utilising by-products of other industries.
items.why: Renewable feedstocks are one of the three green chemistry principles specifically identified in the Study Design. Students need to apply this principle to specific examples such as bioethanol from sugar cane or biodiesel from plant oils.
items.example: Sugar cane is a renewable feedstock that can be harvested within one year. Glucose from sugar cane is fermented to produce bioethanol (C2H5OH), a versatile industrial solvent and fuel, without depleting fossil fuels.

items.title: I can explain how catalysis contributes to sustainable chemical production
items.what: Catalysts increase reaction rate without being consumed. This allows reactions to proceed under milder conditions (lower temperature and pressure), reduces energy consumption, decreases the time needed to obtain products and can reduce by-product formation compared to stoichiometric reagent-based alternatives.
items.why: Catalysis is one of the three green chemistry principles in the Study Design. The development of better catalysts can enable entirely new, more efficient reaction pathways, as demonstrated by the Hoechst ibuprofen synthesis.
items.example: The Hoechst Company process for ibuprofen uses two catalytic steps to complete the synthesis in three steps, compared to the original six-step stoichiometric process by Boots. This reduces waste, lowers cost and improves atom economy.

items.title: I can explain how designing safer chemicals contributes to sustainable chemical production
items.what: Designing safer chemicals means choosing starting materials, reagents and processes that have lower toxicity to humans and animals and a lower environmental impact. This includes replacing hazardous substances with structurally similar, less toxic alternatives where possible.
items.why: This is the third green chemistry principle in the Study Design. Students need to understand that sustainability is not only about energy and waste but also about the health and safety of workers, communities and ecosystems.
items.example: Toluene can replace benzene as a solvent in many organic reactions. Unlike benzene, which is oxidised in the liver to a carcinogen linked to leukaemia, toluene is oxidised to benzoic acid, a non-toxic compound.
